{{Short description|Concept in geometry}}

The concept of [[angle]]s between [[line (geometry)|line]]s (in the [[plane (geometry)|plane]] or in [[Three-dimensional space|space]]), between two planes (''[[dihedral angle]]'') or between a line and a plane can be generalized to arbitrary [[dimension]]s. This generalization was first discussed by [[Camille Jordan]].<ref name= "jordan"/> For any pair of [[flat (geometry)|flats]] in a [[Euclidean space]] of arbitrary dimension one can define a set of mutual angles which are [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] under [[isometry|isometric]] transformation of the Euclidean space. If the flats do not intersect, their shortest [[distance]] is one more invariant.<ref name= "jordan"/> These angles are called '''canonical'''<ref name="afriat"/> or '''principal'''.<ref name="bjoerck"/> The concept of angles can be generalized to pairs of flats in a finite-dimensional [[inner product space]] over the [[complex number]]s.

==Jordan's definition==

Let <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> be flats of dimensions <math>k</math> and <math>l</math> in the <math>n</math>-dimensional Euclidean space <math>E^n</math>.  By definition, a [[translation (geometry)|translation]] of <math>F</math> or <math>G </math> does not alter their mutual angles. If <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> do not intersect, they will do so upon any translation of <math>G</math> which maps some point in <math>G</math> to some point in <math>F</math>. It can therefore be assumed [[without loss of generality]] that <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> intersect.

Jordan shows that [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]] <math>x_1,\dots,x_\rho,</math> <math>y_1,\dots,y_\sigma,</math> <math>z_1,\dots,z_\tau,</math> <math>u_1,\dots,u_\upsilon,</math> <math>v_1,\dots,v_\alpha,</math> <math>w_1,\dots,w_\alpha</math> in <math>E^n</math> can then be defined such that <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> are described, respectively,  by the sets of equations

: <math>x_1=0,\dots,x_\rho=0,</math>

: <math>u_1=0,\dots,u_\upsilon=0,</math>

: <math>v_1=0,\dots,v_\alpha=0</math>

and

: <math>x_1=0,\dots,x_\rho=0,</math>

: <math>z_1=0,\dots,z_\tau=0,</math>

: <math>v_1\cos\theta_1+w_1\sin\theta_1=0,\dots,v_\alpha\cos\theta_\alpha+w_\alpha\sin\theta_\alpha=0</math>

with <math>0<\theta_i<\pi/2,i=1,\dots,\alpha</math>. Jordan calls these coordinates '''canonical'''. By definition, the angles <math>\theta_i</math> are the '''angles''' between <math>F</math> and <math>G</math>.

The non-negative integers <math>\rho,\sigma,\tau,\upsilon,\alpha</math> are constrained by

: <math>\rho+\sigma+\tau+\upsilon+2\alpha=n,</math>

: <math>\sigma+\tau+\alpha=k,</math>

: <math>\sigma+\upsilon+\alpha=\ell.</math>

For these equations to determine the five non-negative integers completely, besides the dimensions <math>n,k</math> and <math> \ell </math> and the number <math>\alpha</math> of angles <math>\theta_i</math>, the non-negative integer <math>\sigma</math> must be given. This is the number of coordinates <math>y_i</math>, whose corresponding axes are those lying entirely within both <math>F</math> and <math>G</math>. The integer <math>\sigma</math> is thus the dimension of <math>F\cap G</math>. The set of angles <math>\theta_i</math> may be supplemented with <math>\sigma</math> angles <math>0</math> to indicate that <math>F\cap G</math> has that dimension.

Jordan's proof applies essentially unaltered when <math>E^n</math> is replaced with the <math>n</math>-dimensional inner product space <math>\mathbb C^n</math> over the complex numbers. (For [[#Angles between subspaces|angles between subspaces]], the generalization to <math>\mathbb C^n</math> is discussed by Galántai and Hegedũs in terms of the below [[#vch|variational characterization]].<ref name="galantai"/>)<ref name= "jordan"/>

==Angles between subspaces==

Now let <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> be [[linear subspace|subspaces]] of the <math>n</math>-dimensional inner product space over the [[real number|real]] or complex numbers. Geometrically, <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> are flats, so Jordan's definition of mutual angles applies. When for any canonical coordinate <math>\xi</math> the symbol <math>\hat\xi</math> denotes the [[unit vector]] of the <math>\xi</math> axis, the vectors <math>\hat y_1,\dots,\hat y_\sigma,</math> <math>\hat w_1,\dots,\hat w_\alpha,</math> <math>\hat z_1,\dots,\hat z_\tau</math> form an [[orthonormality|orthonormal]] [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for <math>F</math> and the vectors <math>\hat y_1,\dots,\hat y_\sigma,</math> <math>\hat w'_1,\dots,\hat w'_\alpha,</math> <math>\hat u_1,\dots,\hat u_\upsilon</math> form an [[orthonormal basis]] for <math>G</math>, where

:<math>\hat w'_i=\hat w_i\cos\theta_i+\hat v_i\sin\theta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,\alpha.</math>

Being related to [[canonical coordinates]], these basic vectors may be called '''canonical'''.

When <math>a_i,i=1,\dots,k</math> denote the canonical basic vectors for <math>F</math> and <math>b_i,i=1,\dots,l</math> the canonical basic vectors for <math>G</math> then the inner product <math>\langle a_i,b_j\rangle</math> vanishes for any pair of <math>i</math> and  <math>j</math> except the following ones.

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \langle\hat y_i,\hat y_i\rangle=1, & & i=1,\dots,\sigma, \\
& \langle\hat w_i,\hat w'_i\rangle=\cos\theta_i, & & i=1,\dots,\alpha.
\end{align}
</math>

With the above ordering of the basic vectors, the [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] of the inner products <math>\langle a_i,b_j\rangle</math> is thus [[diagonal matrix|diagonal]]. In other words, if <math>(a'_i,i=1,\dots,k)</math> and <math>(b'_i,i=1,\dots,\ell)</math> are arbitrary orthonormal bases in <math>F</math> and <math>G</math> then the [[orthogonal transformation|real, orthogonal]] or [[unitary transformation|unitary]] transformations from the basis <math>(a'_i)</math> to the basis <math>(a_i)</math> and from the basis <math>(b'_i)</math> to the basis <math>(b_i)</math> realize a [[singular value decomposition]] of the matrix of inner products <math>\langle a'_i,b'_j\rangle</math>. The diagonal matrix elements <math>\langle a_i,b_i\rangle</math> are the singular values of the latter matrix. By the uniqueness of the singular value decomposition, the vectors <math>\hat y_i</math> are then unique up to a real, orthogonal or unitary transformation among them, and the vectors <math>\hat w_i</math> and <math>\hat w'_i</math> (and hence <math>\hat v_i</math>) are unique up to equal real, orthogonal or unitary transformations applied simultaneously to the sets of the vectors <math>\hat w_i</math> associated with a common value of <math>\theta_i</math> and to the corresponding sets of vectors <math>\hat w'_i</math> (and hence to the corresponding sets of <math>\hat v_i</math>).

A singular value <math>1</math> can be interpreted as <math>\cos\,0</math> corresponding to the angles <math>0</math> introduced above and associated with <math>F\cap G</math> and a singular value <math>0</math> can be interpreted as <math>\cos \pi/2</math> corresponding to right angles between the [[orthogonality|orthogonal]] spaces <math>F\cap G^\bot</math> and <math>F^\bot\cap G</math>, where superscript <math>\bot</math> denotes the [[orthogonal complement]].

==<span class="anchor" id="vch"></span>Variational characterization==

The [[singular value decomposition#vch|variational characterization]] of singular values and vectors implies as a special case a variational characterization of the angles between subspaces and their associated canonical vectors. This characterization includes the angles <math>0</math> and <math>\pi/2</math> introduced above and orders the angles by increasing value. It can be given the form of the below alternative definition. In this context, it is customary to talk of '''principal''' angles and vectors.<ref name="bjoerck"/>

===Definition===
Let <math>V</math> be an inner product space. Given two subspaces <math>\mathcal{U},\mathcal{W}</math> with <math>\dim(\mathcal{U})=k\leq \dim(\mathcal{W}):=\ell</math>, there exists then a sequence of <math>k</math> angles <math> 0 \le \theta_1 \le \theta_2 \le \cdots \le \theta_k \le \pi/2</math> called the principal angles, the first one defined as

: <math>\theta_1:=\min \left\{ \arccos \left( \left. \frac{ |\langle u,w\rangle| }{\|u\| \|w\|}\right) \,\right|\, u\in \mathcal{U}, w\in \mathcal{W}\right\}=\angle(u_1,w_1),</math>

where <math>\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle </math> is the [[inner product]] and <math>\|\cdot\|</math> the induced [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]]. The vectors <math>u_1</math> and <math>w_1</math> are the corresponding ''principal vectors.''

The other principal angles and vectors are then defined recursively via

: <math>\theta_i:=\min \left\{ \left. \arccos \left( \frac{ |\langle u,w\rangle| }{\|u\| \|w\|}\right) \,\right|\, u\in \mathcal{U},~w\in \mathcal{W},~u\perp u_j,~w \perp w_j \quad \forall j\in \{1,\ldots,i-1\} \right\}.</math>

This means that the principal angles <math>(\theta_1,\ldots, \theta_k)</math> form a set of minimized angles between the two subspaces, and the principal vectors in each subspace are orthogonal to each other.

===Examples===

====Geometric example====
Geometrically, subspaces are [[Flat (geometry)|flats]] (points, lines, planes etc.) that include the origin, thus any two subspaces intersect at least in the origin. Two two-dimensional subspaces <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and <math>\mathcal{W}</math> generate a set of two angles. In a three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], the subspaces <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and <math>\mathcal{W}</math> are either identical, or their intersection forms a line. In the former case, both <math>\theta_1=\theta_2=0</math>. In the latter case, only <math>\theta_1=0</math>, where vectors <math>u_1</math> and <math>w_1</math> are on the line of the intersection <math>\mathcal{U}\cap\mathcal{W}</math> and have the same direction. The angle <math>\theta_2>0</math> will be the angle between the subspaces <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and <math>\mathcal{W}</math> in the [[orthogonal complement]] to <math>\mathcal{U}\cap\mathcal{W}</math>. Imagining the angle between two planes in 3D, one  intuitively thinks of the largest angle, <math>\theta_2>0</math>.

====Algebraic example====
In 4-dimensional real coordinate space '''R'''<sup>4</sup>, let the two-dimensional subspace <math>\mathcal{U}</math> be 
spanned by <math>u_1=(1,0,0,0)</math> and <math>u_2=(0,1,0,0)</math>, and let the two-dimensional subspace <math>\mathcal{W}</math> be 
spanned by <math>w_1=(1,0,0,a)/\sqrt{1+a^2}</math> and <math>w_2=(0,1,b,0)/\sqrt{1+b^2}</math> with some real <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> such that <math>|a|<|b|</math>. Then <math>u_1</math> and <math>w_1</math> are, in fact, the pair of principal vectors corresponding to the angle <math>\theta_1</math> with <math>\cos(\theta_1)=1/\sqrt{1+a^2}</math>, and <math>u_2</math> and <math>w_2</math> are the principal vectors corresponding to the angle <math>\theta_2</math> with <math>\cos(\theta_2)=1/\sqrt{1+b^2}.</math>

To construct a pair of subspaces with any given set of <math>k</math> angles <math>\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k</math> in a <math>2k</math> (or larger) dimensional [[Euclidean space]], take a subspace <math>\mathcal{U}</math> with an orthonormal basis <math>(e_1,\ldots,e_k)</math>  and complete it to an orthonormal basis <math>(e_1,\ldots, e_n)</math> of the Euclidean space, where <math>n\geq 2k</math>. Then, an orthonormal basis of the other subspace <math>\mathcal{W}</math> is, e.g.,

: <math>(\cos(\theta_1)e_1+\sin(\theta_1)e_{k+1},\ldots,\cos(\theta_k)e_k+\sin(\theta_k)e_{2k}).</math>

==Basic properties==
* If the largest angle is zero, one subspace is a subset of the other.
* If the largest angle is <math>\pi/2</math>, there is at least one vector in one subspace perpendicular to the other subspace.
* If the smallest angle is zero, the subspaces intersect at least in a line.
* If the smallest angle is <math>\pi/2</math>, the subspaces are orthogonal. 
* The number of angles equal to zero is the dimension of the space where the two subspaces intersect.

==Advanced properties==
* Non-trivial (different from <math>0</math> and <math>\pi/2</math><ref name="Halmos"/>) angles between two subspaces are the same as the non-trivial angles between their orthogonal complements.<ref name="KA06"/><ref name="KJA"/>
* Non-trivial angles between the subspaces <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and <math>\mathcal{W}</math> and the corresponding non-trivial angles between the subspaces <math>\mathcal{U}</math> and <math>\mathcal{W}^\perp</math> sum up to <math>\pi/2</math>.<ref name="KA06"/><ref name="KJA"/>
* The angles between subspaces satisfy the [[triangle inequality]] in terms of [[majorization]] and thus can be used to define a [[distance]] on the set of all subspaces turning the set into a [[metric space]].<ref name="QZL"/>
* The [[sine]] of the angles between subspaces satisfy the [[triangle inequality]] in terms of [[majorization]] and thus can be used to define a [[distance]] on the set of all subspaces turning the set into a [[metric space]].<ref name="KA06"/> For example, the [[sine]] of the largest angle is known as a [[gap between subspaces]].<ref name="Kato"/>

==Extensions==
The notion of the angles and some of the variational properties can be naturally extended to arbitrary [[inner products]]<ref name="KA02"/> and subspaces with infinite [[dimensions]].<ref name="KJA"/>

==Computation==
Historically, the principal angles and vectors first appear in the context of [[canonical correlation]] and were [[Canonical_correlation#Solution | originally computed]] using [[Singular value decomposition|SVD]] of corresponding [[covariance]] matrices. However, as first noticed in,<ref name="bjoerck"/> the [[canonical correlation]] is related to the [[cosine]] of the principal angles, which is [[ill-conditioned]] for small angles, leading to very inaccurate computation of highly correlated principal vectors in finite [[Precision (computer science)|precision]] [[computer arithmetic]]. The [[sine]]-based algorithm<ref name="bjoerck"/> fixes this issue, but creates a new problem of very inaccurate computation of highly uncorrelated principal vectors, since the [[sine]] function is [[ill-conditioned]] for angles close to '''{{pi}}/2.''' To produce accurate principal vectors in [[computer arithmetic]] for the full range of the principal angles, the combined technique<ref name="KA02"/> first compute all principal angles and vectors using the classical [[cosine]]-based approach, and then recomputes the principal angles smaller than '''{{pi}}/4''' and the corresponding principal vectors using the [[sine]]-based approach.<ref name="bjoerck"/> The combined technique<ref name="KA02"/> is implemented in [[open-source]] libraries [[Octave]]<ref>[https://octave.sourceforge.io/octave/function/subspace.html Octave function subspace]</ref> and [[SciPy]]<ref>[https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.subspace_angles.html SciPy linear-algebra function subspace_angles]</ref> and contributed <ref>[https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/54-subspace-m MATLAB FileExchange function subspace]</ref> and 
<ref>[https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/55-subspacea-m MATLAB FileExchange function subspacea]</ref> to [[MATLAB]].
